title: Java Logging APIs and Libraries
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of java logging apis and libraries and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—java.util.logging—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study java logging apis and libraries with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you reduce a failure to a reproducible cause and capture evidence without leaking sensitive data. In this lesson, focus on java.util.logging and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Debug with a reproducible case, inspect a focused stack trace or state snapshot, and change one suspected cause at a time. Logs should support diagnosis without disclosing credentials or private data. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect java.util.logging with slf4j concepts before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: SLF4J concepts
items.text: A useful debugging workflow reproduces the issue, narrows the suspected cause, and records evidence. Logs and diagnostics should explain system behavior without leaking secrets or personal data. Apply that reasoning specifically to slf4j concepts and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test.

items.title: Common logging implementation choices
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Prefer structured, level-appropriate logs and avoid writing secrets or full private payloads. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
